clinicalPearls: Congenital secretory diarrhoea caused by defective intestinal sodium handling, with isolated forms linked to SLC9A3 and activating GUCY2C variants
Presents in the neonatal period with profuse watery diarrhoea and heavy faecal sodium loss
The biochemical picture is high faecal sodium with hyponatraemia and metabolic acidosis, distinguishing it from the alkalosis of congenital chloride diarrhoea
May be preceded antenatally by polyhydramnios and distended bowel loops
A syndromic form associated with SPINT2 features additional congenital anomalies such as choanal or anal atresia
Management relies on aggressive sodium, fluid and bicarbonate replacement to restore balance and support growth
Some patients tolerate gradual weaning of supplementation as intestinal adaptation occurs
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital sodium diarrhoea reflects failure of electroneutral sodium absorption across the intestinal epithelium. Loss-of-function variants in SLC9A3, which encodes the apical sodium/hydrogen exchanger NHE3, impair sodium and fluid reabsorption. Activating variants in GUCY2C (guanylate cyclase 2C) raise intracellular cyclic GMP, inhibiting NHE3 and promoting chloride and fluid secretion, mimicking an enterotoxin-driven state. In both routes luminal sodium and water are retained, producing a secretory diarrhoea with high faecal sodium, systemic sodium depletion, and metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss. The SPINT2-associated syndromic form combines the enteropathy with developmental anomalies.
additionalDifferentials: Microvillus inclusion disease and tufting enteropathy
Cystic fibrosis with intestinal salt loss
Secondary secretory diarrhoea from infection or hormone-secreting tumours
additionalInvestigations: Stool electrolytes showing elevated faecal sodium
Serum electrolytes and acid-base analysis demonstrating hyponatraemia and metabolic acidosis
Faecal osmotic gap to confirm a secretory pattern
Molecular genetic testing for SLC9A3, GUCY2C and SPINT2 variants
Assessment for congenital anomalies in suspected syndromic disease
redFlags: Severe hyponatraemia and dehydration threatening circulation in the neonate
Associated congenital anomalies indicating the syndromic form
Growth failure from inadequate sodium replacement
reference.prognosis: Adequate and sustained sodium, fluid and bicarbonate replacement generally permits satisfactory growth, and some children reduce supplementation over time with intestinal adaptation. Syndromic disease carries added morbidity from associated anomalies.
pitfalls: Confusing the acidotic, high-sodium picture with congenital chloride diarrhoea
Underestimating ongoing sodium losses and under-replacing, causing chronic depletion and poor growth
Overlooking the diagnosis in a neonate with diarrhoea attributed to feed intolerance
Failing to look for associated anomalies that suggest the SPINT2-related syndrome
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Provide aggressive oral and intravenous sodium, fluid and bicarbonate replacement to correct the hyponatraemia, dehydration and metabolic acidosis and restore sodium balance
Optimise nutrition to support normal growth, matching sodium supplementation to ongoing urinary and faecal losses
Monitor serum electrolytes, acid-base status, urinary sodium and growth serially, reducing supplementation over time as intestinal adaptation allows
Identify and surgically manage associated anomalies in the SPINT2 syndromic form, such as choanal or anal atresia
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary team of paediatric gastroenterology, clinical genetics and dietetics
Offer genetic counselling with molecular confirmation of the SLC9A3, GUCY2C or SPINT2 variant to the family
